Structural risk surface

Elevation, slope, and paved-surface cover come from actual USGS 3DEP and NLCD raster measurements where available; stream distance, population, and vulnerability are interpolated from the nearest real historical events. Click anywhere for a location-specific breakdown.

Storm scenario

Changes the storm-level inputs (season, tropical origin) applied across the whole surface. Place-level conditions stay fixed to what's really there.

Illustrative simulation: surrounding terrain relief is already a real input to the base model (all three storm buttons use it), but its fitted linear effect is +0.13 log-odds per standard deviation — the historical data has only one truly extreme episode (Helene) to learn a relief × intensity interaction from. This scenario adds an extra, hypothesis-driven boost proportional to relief on top of the base model's own (small) learned effect, to represent that interaction. Not fitted from data.

Describe a scenario

Uses a real Claude call to read your description when available in this view; otherwise falls back to a comprehensive local phrase interpreter (18 concept categories, ~450 trigger words/phrases, with intensity words like "extremely" and negation like "not urban" both handled) — fully offline, no API needed. Either way, it reports what it applied and why.

What's driving this estimate

Note on imperviousness: this simplified model shows a negative marginal association between paved surface and predicted risk — and this is backed by the real data, not just the model: the most impervious 10% of the 2,637 historical events here (those with a measured imperviousness) had a 1.1% high-consequence rate, versus 7.5% for all of them. Likely reasons include engineered stormwater infrastructure and faster emergency response in developed areas, plus many urban reports being minor nuisance flooding. Nearby flood history is split into two signals for the same reason: more minor flood history nearby lowers predicted risk (resilience/preparedness), while more severe flood history clustered nearby raises it (compounding vulnerability). Fitted log-odds per standard deviation: minor -0.56, severe +0.09. The severe-history effect is small. Surrounding terrain relief (5km) is included too; its fitted effect is +0.13 log-odds per standard deviation. The model's seasonal signal comes from event_month (+0.29) and peak_hurricane_season (+0.46); is_tropical_event is not a model input (it has 1 distinct value in the development events, so it carries no information there). Extreme values are capped before scoring so one outlier feature can't dominate the estimate through linear extrapolation.
11-feature simplified linear model: class-weighted logistic regression fit on 1957 flood events from 2016-2023, with Platt calibration folded into the coefficients. Because both the month and peak-hurricane-season coefficients are positive, a hurricane scenario (September, flag on) scores at least as risky as a typical summer storm (July, flag off) at the same place, by construction; across the 535 mountain flood events, mean predicted risk is 5.5% for the typical scenario and 14.6% for the hurricane scenario (0% of events score lower under the hurricane scenario). Chosen for full client-side transparency. In repeated grouped cross-validation (5x5) on these same 11 features, PR-AUC is 0.20 for this logistic regression and 0.23 for a random forest (no-skill 0.08); on the 697 holdout events from 2024-2026 this model scores PR-AUC 0.34 (no-skill 0.07). The full report's primary model uses 21 features. Not an operational flood warning.
Carolina HighGround — Carolina Data Challenge 2026. Data: NOAA Storm Events, USGS 3DEP & NHD, NCDOT, USGS Annual NLCD, FEMA NRI & CRCI.
